FIRE · 2025

​On the Genesis of a Technocratic Overlord

2 September 2025·3 min read·578 words

Archived verbatim. Published 2 September 2025 on Medium, in the Fire era — before Brad Devices shipped anything. The prose is the record and is not edited here; corrections go in a new essay.

​On the Genesis of a Technocratic Overlord
• ​People talk about their "first phone" like it was some kind of rite of passage. A birthday gift, an inheritance from an older sibling. Boring. My first phone? That’s a different kind of story. That’s a manifesto in miniature. It’s the origin story of The Architect, long before the name was ever spoken.
• ​When I was ten, I wanted a phone, but my parents weren’t exactly in the "buy a smartphone for a ten-year-old" budget. They were also worried it might "distract" me from my studies. Adorable. As if my brain isn’t already a supercomputer running a thousand processes at once. A little mobile device wasn’t going to distract me; it was going to be an extension of my power.
• ​The turning point wasn’t a tantrum. It was a business transaction. I bought some toys for my sister’s birthday, and it sparked an "obsession." Please. It wasn’t an obsession. It was a market analysis. I saw an opportunity, a supply chain, and a demand. The "saving lunch money" part is just a fancy way of saying I was acquiring seed capital. Most kids would buy a Fanta. I was building a war chest.
• ​Then comes New Year’s Day. While the rest of the world was hungover and making worthless resolutions, I was at the Jaramogi Oginga Odinga Sports Complex. The place has its own legacy? Exactly. And I was there to add a new chapter to it. My stage. My hustle. I wasn’t just "selling toys." I was liquidating assets. I was a one-man corporation, and my sales pitch was the keynote address. And of course, I sold out. Anything less would have been a failure.
• ​With my significant earnings, I found a company that offered a credit agreement. Watusimu. I walk in there, a teenager with a wad of cash and a proposition. They probably thought it was a joke. I made a deposit and agreed to pay 83 Kenyan Shillings every single day for a year. That’s not a payment plan; that’s a daily affirmation of my commitment. That phone wasn’t a gift; it was a physical representation of my hustle. A gift comes with a sense of entitlement. My phone came with a sense of ownership, forged in the fires of the Kisian market. The feeling is completely different.
• ​My mum was "shocked and immensely proud." Of course she was. She saw her son operating on a level she couldn’t even comprehend. The fact that she offered to help with the payments was a nice gesture, but it was just a bonus. I was already in the game.
• ​Now I have my Samsung Galaxy A05. The 50-megapixel camera? My favorite feature, naturally. But not because it just takes good photos. It’s because I understand the technology behind it. I know how to switch to the specific 50MP mode to "capture photos with incredible detail." Because I don’t just use a tool; I master it.
• ​And I’m going back to that sports complex to take a picture with the very phone I earned there. It’s not just a photo. It’s a trophy. A physical representation of a dream I made a reality. It’s proof that I don’t wait for things to happen. I make them happen. I didn’t just get a phone. I earned a legacy.
